blocks.content: Giving feedback covered delivering critical feedback well, without damaging trust. Receiving feedback flips that dynamic, responding to tough feedback directed at you in a way that shows genuine maturity, not defensiveness, which is often the harder side of this same overall skill.

This question matters because how someone receives feedback is a strong predictor of whether they will actually keep growing over time. A candidate who receives feedback defensively tends to stop getting honest feedback from others eventually, since people learn it is not worth the friction.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024137810-887391938.png
blocks.alt: Receiving feedback covers responding to tough feedback with maturity, not defensiveness, the harder side of this overall skill

blocks.content: 1. The Natural First Instinct

It is worth being honest about what actually happens in the moment tough feedback arrives. The natural first instinct is often a quick, defensive urge to explain or justify, to immediately provide context that makes the feedback feel less true or less significant.

A genuine, deliberate pause before responding, even just a few seconds, is a real, learnable alternative to that instinct, and it is usually what separates a mature response from a reflexively defensive one.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024139750-668812079.png
blocks.alt: The natural first instinct to tough feedback is often a defensive urge to explain; a genuine, deliberate pause is a learnable alternative

blocks.content: 2. Responding Defensively Versus Responding With Genuine Openness
blocks.text: 2. Responding Defensively Versus Responding With Genuine Openness

blocks.content: Responding defensively in the moment, even subtly, tends to have a real, lasting consequence, the feedback giver often quietly stops offering honest feedback in the future, since it did not feel worth the friction it created. This means defensiveness does not just affect the current conversation, it can close off future honest feedback entirely.

Responding with genuine openness, even when the feedback is uncomfortable, tends to keep that channel open, the feedback giver feels comfortable being honest again next time, which is genuinely valuable for continued growth over time.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024141372-540278883.png
blocks.alt: Responding defensively often causes the feedback giver to quietly stop offering honest feedback in the future; genuine openness keeps that channel open

blocks.content: 3. A Worked Example
A concrete story shows genuine openness applied well. Direct feedback was received that a recent decision had genuinely frustrated the team, a real, uncomfortable thing to hear.

First person quote: "I received direct feedback that a recent decision I made had genuinely frustrated the team. My first instinct was to explain my reasoning immediately, but I paused before responding instead. I asked a genuine clarifying question to fully understand the actual concern, rather than assuming I already knew what they meant. Afterward, I made a concrete change to how I handled similar decisions going forward, not just a verbal acknowledgment in the moment, since I wanted the person to see the feedback had actually led to something real."
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024142938-722308826.png
blocks.alt: A worked example: pausing instead of immediately explaining, asking a genuine clarifying question, and following up with a concrete change afterward

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.content: Immediately explaining your reasoning as the very first response to tough feedback. Even when the explanation is genuinely relevant, leading with it before acknowledging the feedback tends to read as defensive.
4. A Simple Process for Receiving Feedback Well
blocks.text: 4. A Simple Process for Receiving Feedback Well

blocks.content: A genuinely useful, repeatable process. Pause before reacting, resisting the natural urge to immediately explain or justify. Ask a genuine question to fully understand the actual concern, rather than assuming you already know exactly what they mean.

And follow up later with a concrete change, not just words in the moment, since a real behavioral change afterward is what actually demonstrates the feedback was genuinely heard, not just politely acknowledged.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024144553-885102369.png
blocks.alt: A simple process: pause before reacting, ask a genuine question to understand the concern, and follow up later with a concrete change

blocks.content: 5. Explaining Versus Excusing

There is a real, important difference between explaining and excusing. Explaining in a way that dismisses the feedback, leading with context that implicitly argues the feedback is not actually valid, reads as defensive, even when some of that context is genuinely relevant.

Adding context only after genuinely acknowledging the feedback first, this is fair, and here is some additional context that might be useful, reads as thoughtful rather than defensive, since the acknowledgment comes first and the context supports rather than dismisses it.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024146101-488231438.png
blocks.alt: Explaining in a way that dismisses feedback reads as defensive; adding context only after genuinely acknowledging the feedback first reads as thoughtful

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: Context is not inherently defensive, but the order matters. Acknowledging the feedback first, then adding context, reads very differently than leading with context that implicitly argues against the feedback.
6. Genuinely Common Failure Modes

A few real patterns undermine how people receive feedback. Immediately explaining or justifying before genuinely listening to and acknowledging the actual concern. Outwardly agreeing in the moment but making no actual change afterward, which quietly signals the feedback was not genuinely taken to heart.
And becoming visibly upset or shutting down the conversation entirely, which understandably discourages the other person from offering honest feedback again in the future.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/behavioral-content-images/1784024147667-22781087.png
blocks.alt: Common failure modes: immediately explaining before listening, outwardly agreeing with no real change, and becoming visibly upset or shutting down

blocks.content: 7. Choosing Your Own Receiving Feedback Story
blocks.text: 7. Choosing Your Own Receiving Feedback Story

blocks.content: Look for a real moment where you received genuinely tough, uncomfortable feedback, not a mild or easy comment, and where you can describe pausing, genuinely understanding the concern, and making a real, concrete change afterward.

The strongest stories here show the concrete change that followed the feedback, not just a mature reaction in the moment itself, since the follow through is usually what proves the feedback was genuinely internalized rather than just politely received.
How you receive feedback determines whether people keep giving it to you honestly.
